claims.text: Greg Levecchia (co-founder, Bloom Nutrition) asserts that expediting the hiring diligence process for candidates solely because they worked at an admired company is a costly mistake, because employment at a prestigious brand does not establish that the individual was the contributor to that brand's distinctive success.
claims.speaker: Greg Levecchia
conditions: Candidate has recognizable admired company on resume
claims.mechanism: A candidate may have been present at a successful company without being the source of the capabilities or culture that made it successful; accelerating diligence based on brand association skips the screening that would surface this gap.

claims.text: Greg Levecchia observes that when interviewing candidates from admired companies, he was envious of those businesses and let that envy drive him to compress the interview process, which meant the candidate's actual contribution to the admired company's outcomes was never verified.
claims.speaker: Greg Levecchia
conditions: Candidate sourced from a brand the founder admires
claims.mechanism: Envy of an aspirational company creates emotional bias that short-circuits objective evaluation of individual contribution, causing the hiring decision to rest on brand association rather than demonstrated inputs or outputs.

examples.text: Greg Levecchia, co-founder of Bloom Nutrition (a beverage brand tracking toward 150 million cans sold in its first two years), recounts that early in his career he would expedite the interview process whenever a candidate came from a company he admired and was envious of. He discovered the hard way that the glimmering company name on a resume did not mean the individual had contributed the special sauce he was hoping to import into Bloom Nutrition.

practices.text: Never expedite the diligence of your interview funnel just because a candidate has a prestigious or admired company on their resume; hold the same screening standard regardless of brand pedigree.
